subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has demonstrated one thing with which all members will certainly agree. It is that after the next election he will be a great professor of economics or political history back at the University of Saskatoon. It is obvious he does not make his living selling grain on world markets or he would not have spoken as he did, trying to gloss over problems which are on the minds of many who are concerned with grain handling and transportation at the present time in western Canada. All the minister talked about was what the system would be able to do in the future. That is important, it is true, but there is another and more important aspect still. It is what the system can do now. That is what is important to the pocketbooks of prairie farmers. We can all speculate about what is likely to happen in the future, and I am sure that a number of speakers will do so in the course of this debate.
After talking to a good many grain growers, especially from Manitoba, and after talking to representatives of the Wheat Board, I have come to the conclusion that we are facing a crisis in grain transportation as the motion before us suggests. Responsibility for failures which the minister sought to gloss over must be laid at the door of the government itself. After all, the present administration has been in office since 1968, during which time the present situation was developing. Despite the urgency, little action was forthcoming, other than promises.
I should like to spend a few minutes analysing what is happening to grain transportation. Most of the figures I intend to present were obtained from the Wheat Board. They cover the period ending November 11, just this past week. No one in the grain industry really believes these figures are likely to change significantly during the rest of the winter, though some believe the picture is likely to be less satisfactory than those figures suggest.
The Wheat Board has made predictions, as it does each year, concerning the number of grain car unloadings on a weekly basis at Thunder Bay. If the system were operating as well as could be expected, the projection is that 7,000 cars could be unloaded per week. What is actually happening at Thunder Bay is that 5,500 cars of grain are being unloaded per week. During the recent Great Lakes strike grain stocks built up at Thunder Bay, but since the end of that strike three boats have been waiting. The reality is that at the present time there is not enough grain arriving at Thunder Bay to keep the terminals working on a full-time basis.
The Canadian Wheat Board projected that 3,000 to 3,500 cars per week would be unloaded at Vancouver. As of the week of November 11 some 2,400 cars per week have been unloaded. The port of Vancouver has been and will be operating literally from hand to mouth for the remainder of this crop year. As of the end of last week nine ships were waiting at

November 13, 1978
Movement of Grain
Vancouver harbour. Based on what is happening at the present time and on the problems which have become very apparent in the system the projection is that the number of ships which we can expect to be waiting some time in January or February could be in the neighbourhood of 30 or more.
According to the latest Canadian Wheat Board figures, the port of Vancouver will be deferring-or rolling, the term which is used in the industry-some 300,000 to 600,000 tonnes per month, or about 11 million bushels. Those are sales which could be made. In addition, because of problems caused by weather at Prince Rupert, the board is losing sales of an additional 30,000 tonnes per week.
What has happened to the grain transportation system in this country is that it has been allowed to slide into such a state of ineffectiveness that the system does not have any surge capacity. It cannot handle any additional sales opportunities which may, from time to time, be thrust upon it. The truth is that the situation is getting worse every year. Elevators are very nearly full and terminals are less than half full. Producer stocks on the farm are up some 20 per cent. Farmers are holding more grain than they did last year. If the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board and for transportation had to make his income from grain he had to sell through the quota system to the Canadian Wheat Board, he certainly would not have spoken the way he did this afternoon.
At the present time the Canadian Wheat Board is actually working harder at deferring wheat sales than it is at selling grain. That is the state of the industry in 1978.
I am especially concerned about the province of Manitoba. The grain being sold by the Wheat Board at the present time is number one wheat. Movement of that grain is primarily out of Saskatchewan, the tip of southwestern Manitoba and parts of Alberta. Because of this, very little grain is moving out of the remainder of Manitoba. The reason for that is that the grade of grain in Manitoba has not been as high as it is in parts of Saskatchewan. By the Wheat Board's own admission, movement of grain out of the province of Manitoba will be almost non-existent until the first part of January 1979.
Elevators in Manitoba are full. Farmers have very little, if any, cash flow, and the cash advances farmers can get from the Canadian Wheat Board are so small that they are almost useless in terms of the amount of money it takes to operate a modern grain farm. How does the government or any part of the grain industry expect the Manitoba farmer to pay his bills in a time of rising expenses?
Barley is not being sold because number one wheat is the only grain which is being moved. The Wheat Board has said that it has backed away from barley sales. The Board does not even use the expression "deferred barley sales". The Board says it has backed away from barley sales. The government must obviously share much of the blame for this because it has had opportunities to make changes and to accept recommendations.
The railways have also entered into the fray. The problem has been confused. For example, CPR says it has all kinds of

hopper cars and boxcars and that it does not need additional rolling stock. CNR says it does not have enough rolling stock. This confuses the matter and makes it difficult to distinguish the real crux of the problem. The Canadian Wheat Board feels that 4,000 hopper cars are need immediately. The board would like to see a total hopper car fleet of about 20,000 cars in ten to 15 years.
The 1978-79 shipping season looks truly dismal. There will be hundreds of millions of dollars in lost sales. The grain industry is already talking that way. There will be large demurrage payments. That is inevitable. That is coming, as sure as winter comes to the prairies.
Farmers will be frustrated because they will have very little cash with which to operate their farms. This will be especially so for exclusively grain farmers. We might even see China becoming a traditional customer of the United States, if the situation is not corrected relatively quickly.
In view of what I have stated it is no wonder that the present government's electoral fortunes on the prairies are so dismal. Rail problems have mounted while this government has been in power. The Liberal government has done little more than study these problems, and it must bear the blame for the loss of millions of dollars in sales.
Some days ago the minister said to me that the Wheat Board is studying continuous seven-day a week operations. He also said that there are problems with labour unions. Both those statements are true, but the whole question is really academic because there is not enough grain being delivered to Thunder Bay to allow it to be unloaded around the clock on a seven-day a week basis.
The big challenge which we as a country will be facing will be the tremendous leap in capacity which will be necessary to meet increased export opportunities by 1985 and even by 1990. Because of delay and lack of action by this government in moving to a rational grain handling approach, we will have to accomplish this in a very short period of time at possibly much greater cost to the government, industry, and farmers than should be the case. We could have developed this rational grain handling approach over a longer period of time if there had been more rational planning.
Foreign demand for Canadian grain will increase, as will foreign demand for grain from other countries. France is said to be planning a 67 per cent increase in grain exports by 1985. The United States Feed Grain Council thinks its exports will increase by some 50 per cent in the next four years, while Japan and China are said to need between 40 per cent and 50 per cent more production or, very likely, imports by 1985. Canadian Wheat Board officials have said that they feel that these intentions, along with the goals of both the importing and exporting nations, are a positive proof of trends in the grain industry which will certainly continue into the next decade. This is an additional reason why Canada must act quickly to protect its traditional markets, let alone develop new markets to widen the variety of Canadian grain products. Certainly the loss in sales over the past 12 months to the
November 13, 1978

People's Republic of China is an indication of the kind of action the industry and the government must avoid.
If we look into the future there is no question that grain will be one of the major export dollar earners for Canada. In fact, for any of the major exporting countries grain will be one of the major export dollar earners. In my opinion, we must make a commitment to move the kind of grain and volume of grain required. The dollars invested in the grain industry will be numerous but the invested return on those dollars will be four or five times greater than the original investment. Time is of the essence and action must be taken now.
What should be done? The government has spent a large amount of money on numerous studies, but one which we consider to be especially good is the Hall commission report. I believe that action should be taken immediately on some of the recommendations in that report. We, as a party, had hoped that the prairie rail authority, the establishment of which was the cornerstone of the Hall commission report, would have been instituted. Had the prairie rail authority, rather than the Prairie Rail Action Committee which the government established, been instituted, it would have given an over-all coordinated approach to the grain transportation problems in the country. However, that has not taken place because of the reluctance of the transport minister to do anything in terms of that recommendation.
We feel that another recommendation of the Hall commission should have been adopted, that is, that the railways be compensated for the cost of moving grain by rail. Railways must also be responsible for adequate maintenance and upgrading of the lines now within the basic network, or which would be added to the basic network. The latest costing report by the Snavely commission is out and it shows that the cost of shipping grain under the Crowsnest pass rate totalled some $354 million. The railways' cost came to $175 million, the farmers' cost came to $115 million, and the federal government's cost came to $64 million. In view of those costs, I do not think anyone would suggest that the railways could devote much time and money to moving grain at the statutory rate. They lose money on every bushel that is shipped, and the more grain they move, the more they lose. Farmers and farm organizations and governments should not expect the situation to improve. In fact it will only get worse in the months and years to come. When you think of all the problems we have had this year, just think of what will happen in a few years from now if the government continues to adopt the same system.
We on this side of the House believe that the railways should be compensated for hauling grain. We also believe that farmers should continue to receive the benefits of the Crowsnest pass rate, and in return for the money received for hauling Canadian grain, the railways should upgrade western rail lines. We think expenditures should be made on parallel rail lines in certain areas in western Canada, mainly in the mountain
Movement of Grain
areas. We also think that stop-off charges in most cases should be eliminated in moving grain in western Canada.
We believe that the principle of the off line elevators should be adopted as a realistic alternative in those areas of Western Canada that do not have rail service. We also believe that money should be spent in the area of ports and terminals. Expenditures should be made, for example, on dredging at Thunder Bay, on Canadian Wheat Board co ordinators for all grain going through Thunder Bay and on enabling the Canadian Wheat Board to play a more prominent role in the over-all co-ordination of grain movement on the prairies. We believe that all these recommendations should be adopted if we are going to move grain in the volumes mentioned by the minister, by us on this side, and by the NDP. So far the government has shown itself to be sloppy and lacklustre when it comes to most things, but especially in grain transportation.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me say that this year the country will lose hundreds of millions of dollars because we cannot fill our export commitments. That amount of money would buy many hopper cars. We will end up with large demurrage charges and with economic hardship for western farmers. We will also have a loss in foreign dollars to Canada because of losses in sales in western Canada. This is the legacy that the minister and the government will leave to the western grain farmer-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate this afternoon. This is a timely motion, but I am surprised that it is the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), a member of the NDP, who should bring forth this motion and cry crocodile tears for farmers in western Canada, remembering that ten days or two weeks ago when a bill was before the House legislating the marine engineers back to work, whose strike was costing the farmers in the Wheat Board area some $10 million a day, the NDP voted against it. They voted against a bill which would mean money in the pockets of western farmers, despite the fact that the premier of the province of Saskatchewan, a New Democratic Party member,

November 13, 1978
Movement of Grain
had sent a wire to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asking him to legislate the workers back to work.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre was shedding crocodile tears today. When western farmers learn the way the New Democratic Party voted on that piece of legislation, they will have second thoughts about what those members are doing in Ottawa.
Previous members have supplied many statistics to the House, and I do not propose to go into all of them. The situation in western Canada is very serious. Country elevators are bulging at the seams. The stocks in the terminal elevators in Thunder Bay and on the west coast are low. The movement of grain by railways ranges from 50 per cent to 70 per cent capacity. We have received reports of a deferral in deliveries of some 1.5 million tonnes, cancellation of contracts, and lost sales. The producers in western Canada have lost hundreds of millions of dollars.
For the first time in four years China has purchased wheat from the United States amounting to some 2.5 million tonnes, grain which the farmers of western Canada could have and traditionally would have sold to China. The reason China looked to the United States was because Canada could not guarantee delivery. The figure of the loss to the prairie farmer is not available. If one spent time going through all the papers and listening to the speeches made by representatives of the Canadian Wheat Board and other organizations, one might determine the losses. The producers and members of parliament should know the facts.
On November 7 I asked the minister to make a statement on motions setting out in detail the situation as far as sales, deferrals, and lost sales was concerned. The minister declined to do so, saying that the Canadian Wheat Board had made these facts available to the producers, that it was the appropriate body, and that he did not feel it was up to him to give this report to parliament. It is his responsibility to do so, but of course he has been very busy. He wears three hats as Minister of Justice, Minister of Transport, and minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang). I do not envy him his job. Those three portfolios are more than any man can handle. It is vital that the Prime Minister take immediate steps to divide those responsibilities so that whoever takes charge of the various portfolios can do a proper job.
The grain handling and transportation system is important and vital to the economy not only of western Canada but of Canada as a whole. It brings in billions of dollars in foreign exchange each year. It has a multiplier effect of some 5.5 times the amount which comes into the country, and a domino effect which spurs the economy of the whole country. Yet we continue to lose millions and millions of dollars in sales. Why has this happened?
Why is the grain handling and transportation system in such chaos? One only has to read the report of the agricultural task force of 1969 which was commissioned by this government. At that time it indicated that there was no future in the grain
trade. That was the essence of its report. The task force recommended getting rid of half the farm acreage and two out of three farmers. The government brought in the LIFT program and paid farmers not to grow grain, a form of stabilization program which did not make sense, and a small farm program, and other programs developed to do what the agricultural task force suggested. Later the Prime Minister told the farmers in western Canada to sell their own wheat. He said, "Sell your own wheat".
If we look back over the past few years, we find that there have been a series of studies and royal commissions. Many of their recommendations were ignored by the government. There was the Hall commission report, the Snavely commission, and others. The Hall commission report was an excellent one on the grain handling and transportation system in western Canada. Mr. Justice Hall made some excellent recommendations, one of which was the setting up of the Prairie Rail Authority. Of course that recommendation was ignored by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. Instead he set up the Prairie Rail Action Committee.
The functions of the proposed Prairie Rail Authority were to examine lines which Mr. Justice Hall said were in doubt, listen to representations, and to monitor these lines to see whether they should remain. But the minister set up the Prairie Rail Action Committee which made a final report and a holus bolus decision to shut down lines, without study and input from the people concerned: the railways, the elevators, and the people on the lines. The chairman of PRAC has indicated that there was too much mileage in the basic network recommended by Mr. Hall. Mr. Hall was not even invited to meet with the minister in charge of the Wheat Board for almost a year. He would not have been invited if it had not been for the fact that members of the opposition were able to pass a resolution in the Standing Committee on Agriculture which requested Mr. Justice Hall to appear before it. Then the minister in charge of the Wheat Board decided to meet with Mr. Justice Hall.
Another of the recommendations of Mr. Justice Hall was the utilization of inland terminals to service primarily the port of Churchill, which I am sure the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) will speak about later, as well as the port of Prince Rupert. Now the minister is putting the elevators and government inland terminals up for sale with no explanation as to why they are to be sold. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), in a statement which he issued, said that selling the government elevators would save the sum of S8.3 million. This was at a time when the elevators at Moose Jaw and Saskatoon were being utilized to maximum capacity and were showing larger profits than ever before. The general manager of the inland terminal system said that he could not understand where the President of the Treasury Board got the figure of $8.3 million because the system, he said, would earn between $4 million and $4.5 million.
I was interested to read in the supplementary estimates which were tabled in this House a few days ago, at page 10

November 13, 1978

under vote 20a, that deducted from the estimates that are supplemental funds available from vote 45 amounting to $930,000, which amount is due to cancellations in respect of the planned sale of Canadian government grain elevators. On the one hand the President of the Treasury Board says that selling these elevators will save $8.3 million; on the other hand the estimates indicate a saving of $930,000. I do not understand it.
It is also interesting to note that we are doing away with the inland terminals in the west but building new terminals in eastern Canada. I received a news release the other day to the effect that four or five elevator companies or private concerns will receive either grants or loans to build terminals in eastern Canada. Two years ago this House passed estimates of $8 million to help build a terminal elevator sponsored by the Ontario co-operatives for the purpose of servicing an oil seeds plant that would be built alongside it in the Windsor area. The oil seeds plant was not viable unless the elevator was built; therefore the government provided $8 million to help and this was at a time when oil seeds plants in western Canada were having difficulty surviving.
The government is not interested in the viability of the agricultural industry in western Canada. They have decided to sell these inland terminals at a price which nobody knows. We do not know if there is a reserve bid or what will happen if they are not sold. We do not know what will happen to the employees.
Both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board have said in the past that these elevators are underutilized. It is true that they are being used only at 20 per cent to 25 per cent of their capacity, but even so a profit has been made. They contend that the reason these elevators have been underutilized is due to the wheat pools and UGG, but it is interesting to note that the elevators in Moose Jaw and Saskatoon are being utilized to capacity now, mostly by the pools.
I do not believe that the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board have ever sat down and discussed the utilization of those elevators with either the railways or the farm organizations. They are all part of the system which the minister spoke about. Whoever buys the terminals will have to recover from the farmer the interest costs of the purchase price and the capital costs. It may be said that the capital costs should not be taken into consideration, but if the elevators are purchased by a company they must at least recover their investment as determined at the time of sale. These elevators were built in the 1920s.
The elevators should be utilized fully after consultation with the line company elevators, the railways and the farm organizations by supplying their services to the various grain companies at cost. By "cost" I mean the actual cost of operation and cost of keeping the elevators in good repair. The government cannot include capital costs because they have been written off many times over. If this were done, grain could be moved through the system faster to the export position, we would not
Movement of Grain
be faced with bottlenecks on the west coast or with demurrage charges, and there would be a more even flow of grain.
The New Democratic Party has suggested that the government call upon the railways to add 4,000 hopper cars to their fleets. The government has already supplied some 8,000 hopper cars to the railways at no cost to them except that they must keep the hopper cars in good repair. It is my understanding that at the present time the railways are operating at between 50 per cent and 75 per cent capacity. I suggest that possibly we do not need any more hopper cars but instead we should take a look at the utilization of cars, whether they be hopper cars or boxcars.
Perhaps the Wheat Board should, if the minister will not, sit down with the elevator companies, the railways and the farm organizations to determine how they can best utilize the system. I do not believe such a thing has ever been done. There are many other things that could be done in the system through the co-operation of the various organizations and components. This has been the problem, a lack of cohesiveness.
If the grain could be delivered to the west coast or Thunder Bay on time it would save many millions of dollars in demurrage charges. The minister in answer to questions put to him regarding demurrage charges says, "Oh well, we never know when the boats are coming in." He talks as though the boats float out of the sky and land in the harbour. I suggest that these boats are at sea for some considerable time and are always in contact by radio. Contracts are made weeks and months in advance, and the Wheat Board and elevators know when these boats will be coming in.
In closing, I would say that we in Canada have the potential to produce a lot more grain. We have the potential to deliver that grain to export position if the various components of the system would only co-operate and if the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Minister of Agriculture would do their jobs. The markets are available and more will be available. There is a need for more and more food in the world. But if we continue to lose our reputation for delivering grain, then we will continue to lose the markets. The effects on the economy not only of western Canada but of the whole of Canada will be very drastic.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate briefly in this debate in order to tell the people of western Canada that we in the east and particularly in southwestern Ontario have concern for them and their problems.
The lament of gloom and doom is with us again in this debate, Mr. Speaker. For the last few years the people of Canada have been told how tough, how really bad, things are. I begin to wonder whether the politicians in this House and the media across the country understand the situation or ever ask people individually what the problems are.
I bring this point up very sincerely because I think one of the problems in Canada today is an illusion of things going bad. This illusion has been fostered by the opposition parties

November 13, 1978
Movement of Grain
and in some cases by the media. They have been trying to spread the impression that things are very bad and that this is a very bad government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Well, I should like to comment on the New Democratic Party for a moment. This party is supposed to be backed by labour, is supposed to be leading labour and wants the responsibility that labour could give them after the next election. On two occasions recently, however, the party completely forgot about the people of Canada, once during the marine strike and once during the post office strike. I feel this fact should be brought to the attention of everybody in Canada. If I remember correctly, and I could be mistaken, two and a half or three years ago parliament was recalled to deal with an emergency concerning the grain handlers. On that occasion the NDP again stuck with one particular segment of the country and forgot about the rest of the country.
I will read today's motion just to clarify matters. It says:
That this House condemns the government for its failure:
(a)	to require the railroads to add 4,000 hopper cars and 5,000 repaired boxcars to their grain fleet; and
(b)	to give the Canadian Wheat Board total authority to co-ordinate all aspects of grain movement and any other authority necessary to protect and expand grain exports.
On the one hand the opposition are concerned about grain exports, yet on the other hand they will vote in the House against a motion designed to get products to the export market. This leaves me a little confused. I hope the people of Canada will note this, however, and not forget it at the next election.
I should like to turn now to the condemnation of government policy by the official opposition. In the past two or three years their practice seems to have been to condemn everything. The acquisition of hopper cars was mentioned briefly by the opposition but they maintain they would have done more. In the past the cabinet has recognized the deteriorating condition of the boxcar fleet and has purchased 8,000 hopper cars made up as follows: 2,000 in 1973; 4,000 in 1974 and in 1975, and 2,000 in 1977, at a cost of approximately $260 million. The opposition did not mention that nor the evident success of the program.
These cars have had a significant impact upon the movement of grain as the grain farmers well know. Some of the commitments made to the western farmers will not only help them but help the farmers of eastern Canada as well. I want to say to grain farmers in the west that we in the east are very concerned about them and their problems. When I return to my riding of Middlesex-London-Lambton and hear comments about the problems of the farmers in Canada, I know that although the eastern farmer understands the problems of the western farmer, sometimes there is a lack of communication between them. The farm organizations meet once or twice a

year. I think some of the misunderstandings between east and west could be resolved in the farming community. They have much in common. They depend on the weather, they depend on the soil, they depend on the use of the proper fertilizer; they have a common denominator. All this could serve to unify Canada in the way we all want to see it unified.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) mentioned that over the last ten years this government has done nothing that will be beneficial to farmers in western Canada in the future. I disagree. I think that under the direction of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), who is in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, more has been done than was done by anyone who previously held that position. It is very easy to say that more should be done, but I think credit should be given for accomplishments. There is only a certain amount of money available to all the ministries and the 28 or 30 cabinet ministers try hard to get their share of the funds.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have great respect for the opposition finance critic. He is probably one of the greatest opposition finance critics and I may say that I hope he keeps that position for some time. I notice he takes an interest in the farmers as well as ail other areas that come within his purview. It is amazing that one man can know so much about everything yet never give credit to the government for anything it has done since he has been finance critic. With all this heckling from the opposition, Mr. Speaker, I think I must have hit the core of the problem. It may be a possibility that when the next speaker from the official opposition steps up to express his opinions on this particular motion, he may say at the beginning of his remarks: "You are doing a good job;" but I will not hold my breath. It does not matter if there are a lot of boxcars and a lot of special grain cars, without the tracks to run them on there is a problem. Neither does it matter what expenditure is made on hopper cars. In the recent past, while the Government of Canada has certainly gone ahead strongly on the rehabilitation of branch lines, the rehabilitation and upgrading of the system cannot be carried out until the size and extent of the basic network is known. A start has to be made some place, but it has been let go. I would agree partially with some of the criticism that has been voiced. It has been let go, and maybe for too long. But at this particular time
November 13, 1978

we are moving ahead to make it better than before, and as well looking forward to the next 30 or 40 years.
If I may digress for a moment, we are not as aggressive as we should be. I think in the future Canada will be in a similar position to that of the OPEC nations. I can see in the future the importance of the food dollar with Canada being the centre of the food dollar chain because of Canada's great areas of agricultural land and also because of the productivity of the farmer. I was talking to a farmer the other day in my riding of Middlesex-London-Lambton, just outside of Strathroy, and I said to him: "You are producing so much now; how much could you produce if you had to?" He replied: "If we were pressed to increase our productivity, we could maybe increase it by 150 to 200 times and have the same product we have now." Obviously the farmers are producing; there is no question about that. The figure is 100 per cent in the last ten years. They are the type of people who would do so providing they are compensated in the proper coin of the realm. Sometimes I question whether they are but I think farmers are in an improving position.
Regarding branch line rehabilitation, almost 50 per cent of the existing prairie rail network can carry only boxcars. It is essential to upgrade the lines to be retained in order to gain full impact from the use of the heavier loading hopper cars. New hopper car acquisition must be co-ordinated with improvements to the system. Seventy million dollars has been allocated for this program for the next year.
To date the following improvements have been carried out. Two subdivisions have been upgraded to carry fully loaded hopper cars. Cut widening and track stabilization has been carried out on approximately nine subdivisions. This will help to reduce problems caused by snow drifting and soft tract in the spring and fall. Many of the lines concerned were built to very low standards in the first place and such work represents a permanent, lasting improvement. Because of these expenditures I think we are at the beginning of great things for the western farmer. I believe the farmers' production will increase in proportion to the facilities that we have available in Canada. This will help the export market.
Returning to the question of being critical of government and critical of the Canadian people, we do not realize what we can do until we have to. In the past Canadians have had fairly secure and good lives. Different government agencies have helped out in certain areas. We never get complaints about that, and why should we? We are trying to help people to be more productive, thus making Canada a better country and a leader in the world's export markets.
Permafrost research is being carried out on the Churchill line to establish ways and means to stabilize the subgrade. This section of line, which is unique in the world for its permafrost problems, will remain at boxcar standards until the early 1980s when stability problems will have been resolved. A party of permafrost experts from many parts of the world, including the Soviet Union and the People's Republic of
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
China, toured the lines this summer. We were seeking the best expert advice available.
Why did we do that? Canada is a complex country. It is a country of differing climates, attitudes and feelings. The most important thing we have in Canada is our land. We have a lot to learn yet about our land. I do not think enough research has been done in that respect. The government is doing more in the area of observation and spending money to make sure that these particular things are good not only for the present but for the next generation and the next century.
In summary, the rehabilitation program will eventually ensure that we have a basic network secure to the year 2000 that will not suffer from winter disruptions by reason of snow drifting. It will not suffer from soft track and drainage problems in the spring and fall. It will not suffer from rail buckling problems in the summer. It will be capable of carrying aluminum hopper cars unrestricted. In short, the rehabilitation program will greatly assist the utilization of the current rail car fleet.
We must recognize that there are problems. Certainly the government has worked very hard to solve them, and it will continue to work to solve these problems not only for this generation of grain farmers but for all grain farmers in the future. This government is thinking not only of today but of the future of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which is somewhat similar to the question of privilege referred to by my colleague, but much more specific. On three occasions during the question period today, ministers of the Crown misled this House by indicating that a certain transaction had been completed, by either a subsidiary or a Crown corporation known as Petro-Can, and that there was no charge against the resources of the Government of Canada as a result of this transaction.
In reply to a specific question raised by my colleague from Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) stated: "Mr. Speaker, I made it very clear that this was a commercial transaction. It was negotiated and financed by normal commercial instrument. There are no government guarantees."
At another point, in response to a question put by my colleague from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), a similar comment was made. In response to a question put by myself to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), dealing specifically with the nature of this transaction, the Minister of Finance stated that "it is a commercial transaction.. . This was analysed by those who were loaning the money. They found that the assets being given against borrowing were very good indeed."
The act incorporating Petro-Can could not be more clear. They act as an agent of the Crown. In similar circumstances, the Export Development Corporation has legal opinions which state in that case that the Crown is bound by every obligation entered into by the Export Development Corporation.
We will be looking into this more fully. However, I would like to give Your Honour notice that we think we have a most substantial question of privilege to be raised at the earliest opportunity.
Is it agreed that we take this as notice?
Agreed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on the NDP motion moved by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) is very important. It is an important topic for all members of the House, particularly those from western Canada. This debate has dealt with a number of circumstances and situations dating back not only to the four or five years I have been here, but many years beyond. That is as good an indication as any that the problems which plague the grain industry do not go away but recur, not only for the grain producer but for the grain industry as a whole.
Hon. members who took part in the debate referred to two issues that continually arise. I refer to labour unrest, strikes in various sectors and by various unions involved with or affecting the movement of grain. That has been referred to by most members who have spoken today. The second is natural disasters, such as extreme snowstorms which plagued a number of branch lines in western Canada last year and the torrential rains in British Columbia this fall which washed out the rail line to Prince Rupert. That will disrupt the movement of grain to that port, as well as shipping and the programs of the Wheat Board and grain companies. Those two situations continue to recur.
I thought either the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre or the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) might have recognized the tremendous progress made over the past eight to ten years in resolving some of the problems which cause difficulty to the grain farmer and grain producer. As usual, opposition members have totally disregarded the tremendous advances made over the years in solving these problems, learning what causes them and dealing effectively with them. Producers and organizations are more effectively involved in developing policies and solutions to many problems that have been with us for a long time.
Hon. members forget the years not so long ago of very poor sales and very poor prices, when there was no real policy on domestic feed grains. It is not so many years ago that damp barley in Saskatchewan next to the Alberta border was 25 cents or 30 cents a bushel; that was in the late 1960s. Next door in Provost and Camrose in Alberta, just across the border, it brought twice that much purely because of a regulation which had been in existence for years of not allowing trade in grain under the Wheat Board between the provinces. So we have seen the clearing away of an awful lot of that kind of pure nonsense which was certainly a hindrance to the development of normal trade and sales as far as grain was concerned.
Many hon. members opposite, whether the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil),
November 13, 1978

the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) or others, if they were to go back into their constituencies, as I know they do, and travel up and down the grid roads and municipal roads of their constituencies and compare the situation today of their farmer friends, their grain producer friends they have known for years, as I can certainly do in my area, with the economic situation in those very farmyards ten or 15 years ago, I am certain they will find a great difference.
Life then was a great deal tougher than it is today. I suppose that in essence what 1 am saying is this, that while there are problems in the field of grain handling and transportation as well as in grain production generally, there are far fewer problems than there were. In the meantime, despite those problems the grain producer over the last several years has enjoyed an economic benefit which neither he nor any of us in this chamber in any political party might have believed possible five or six years ago. If hon. members from various rural constituencies would do what I suggested, drive through their own areas and look at some of the farm operations and compare them with conditions eight or ten years ago on smaller holdings, contrasting their net worth today with their net worth eight, ten or even 15 years ago, they will find that-

-despite inflation and even with an 85-cent dollar they are still immeasurably better off than their brothers who may be working in a small town as mechanics, or working in Calgary or other places. The hon. member for Moose Jaw, I think it was, applied some interesting logic which to my mind was somewhat inconsistent with proceedings earlier in the day when there was great opposition from hon. members opposite to more Canadian ownership in the oil industry.

speechtext: Not at all.

speechtext:
That is the truth. There is no question about what was involved. They are not concerned or interested in Canadian ownership or government involvement in that area. Yet when it comes to the grain industry, which has traditionally been owned by Canadian farmer-producers, the opposition take a different stance. Years ago the Canadian government put up a number of storage elevators on the prairies, and it seems to me that there really is not very much need to continue inland terminal storage. Major companies which are Canadian-owned, farmer-owned, are engaged in the storage business, as I say, and it seems to me that in an industry which is highly government regulated in any event it makes sense for those elevators, whether they be in Moose Jaw, Saskatoon or elsewhere, to be under the control and jurisdiction of the grain companies themselves.

The hon. member for Moose Jaw was very concerned that the government should be getting out of that operation, yet earlier in the day the Conservative opposition was very concerned that the government should be getting into the energy business in an effort to ensure adequate supplies of energy at a reasonable price for prairie farmers.

speechtext: What price would you sell them for?

speechtext:
The price and the arrangements can certainly be negotiated, and I am sure both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the minister responsible for the Wheat Board have already held discussions with grain companies and other interested groups in that regard. It seems to me to make a great deal of sense to place those facilities under the jurisdiction of the grain companies themselves.
The motion before us condemns the government for its failure to require the railroads to add 4,000 hopper cars and
5,000	repaired boxcars to the grain fleet. It goes on to say the Wheat Board should be given total authority to co-ordinate all aspects of grain movement and any other authority necessary to protect and expand grain exports. I am sure that on reflection the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre might wish to modify some of the wording of that motion. 1 am sure he does not really want to bring all aspects of the industry under the Wheat Board. He might wish to extend the Board's authority, but I do not believe he would want to see the government or the Wheat Board or any other agency getting into the movement of grain from farm to farm, from farm to feed-lot, what might be termed community sales.
It seems to me that more attention should be paid to the progress which has been achieved in terms of grain movement and storage. This aspect has been touched on by the minister and by some other speakers. It is not only a matter of more boxcars or hopper cars. There are factors involved in grain movement quite aside from boxcars. I am sure most hon. members are aware of the advantages of the hopper cars over the old-fashioned boxcars. In my view, we could use still more but I would question the advisability of turning the money over to the railroads, as was suggested in the Hall commission report and again this afternoon by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, for the purchase of the cars and for the re-grading which must take place if many of these branch lines are to be able to carry those hopper cars. Repairing all those branch lines is a big job. There is a good deal of that going on now.
I am more than happy to see what is going on in my part of Saskatchewan, and I am sure other hon. members are too. On weekends when I go home, I see rebuilding, re-gravelling and new equipment. Going from Saskatoon to North Battleford I see 50 to 60 tanker or ballast cars hauling ballast out to those lines to get them rebuilt. That is a big program which will cost an estimated $700 million. That program will go on into the 1980s before it is completed. About $70 million is projected to be spent in the forthcoming fiscal year. Almost $100 million

November 13, 1978

has been allocated or spent this year for new equipment and for upgrading.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) and the authors of the Hall report suggest that this government should merely turn over to the railroad companies those large chunks of cash necessary to make grain hauling an economic operation, and that we should ask the railroads to go out and buy boxcars and rebuild rail lines. When they make that suggestion, they are really not looking at the facts and the history of the last eight or ten years.
I remind hon. members of the last time the National Transportation Act was amended by a minority parliament in the 1960s. One of the solutions to the problem of upgrading rail lines at that time was thought to be a provision to allow the railroads to apply to abandon branch lines on which they were loosing money, which, of course, they did. They applied to abandon many lines. The solution decided upon by parliament, which met the approval of most parties in this House ten or 12 years ago, was to say that the treasury should pay by way of branch line subsidies to the railroads the amount of the loss which was estimated. What happened to that subsidy? It grew to be about $100 million in the past year. The money went to the railroads, but did it go to the rebuilding of branch lines? Of course it did not.

speechtext: My hon. friend says they took the money and ran. That is why I go back to the point I made earlier. I wonder why my hon. friend gets up, as he did today, and suggests to the government that we continue to pour in $100 million or $200 million a year with no strings attached.

This is the suggestion I gathered the hon. member made in his remarks, as did other hon. members opposite. The experience of the last number of years demonstrates to me that the Hall commission made a mistake with that recommendation. I suggest the hon. member is wrong in endorsing it. We cannot give the money directly to the railroads with no strings attached and expect them to build boxcars and rail lines and haul grain. They have not done that in the past, and I am not sure what has changed which would ensure that they will do that in the future.
That is why I endorse the approach taken by the minister, his department and the government in terms of providing funds for specific purposes; for example, the purchase of hopper cars, rebuilding and upgrading equipment or rebuilding specific lines, either CN or CP. The money should be paid when the job is done. It seems to me that is a much better approach than to expect them, as we have in the past-and we

were disappointed-to take that money and make the improvements all of us want to see in the grain handling network.
I mentioned that in the past that not only has the government purchased 8,000 hopper cars, but we have also rationalized the whole rail network. Hon. members will be aware that a problem and an issue for years and years has been the threat of rail and branch line abandonment. That threat has largely been removed and cleared away by the Hall recommendations and that commission's handling of that entire question. There are still some lines which are being dealt with by the Prairie Rail Action Committee.

speechtext: That is the problem.

speechtext:
It will not be a problem much longer because that committee's report will be in by the end of the year, and we will finally know what its recommendations are. There will still be an opportunity for the hon. member, for me and for other hon. members to make recommendations to the minister in that respect if we do not like some of the committee's recommendations. Of those lines in doubt, which used to add up to 8,000 or 10,000 miles, today there are less than 2,000 miles of lines in doubt and they are still being dealt with by the Prairie Rail Action Committee. In that respect we have come a long way.
Hon. members referred to improvements in car utilization and in car turnaround. There has been improvement in this regard, and there are railroad figures to demonstrate that. We are moving much more today with the same number of cars and the same kind of equipment than we did in 1974. We are moving about 30 per cent more, but I am sure many hon. members of all parties will also agree that we could continue to improve that car turnaround and car utilization in order to get more mileage out of the equipment which we have in operation.
There have been improvements to the terminal elevator system. At Vancouver expansion is going forward. That in itself will assist a great deal. I think hon. members are aware that there are other bottlenecks associated with getting grain to Vancouver. These are being worked on, and gradually the list of difficulties over the last number of years has been narrowed down quite considerably.
I do not say we do not still have problems. I just say that the system has been substantially improved. I agree that there are improvements yet to be made, and they will be made as the various segments work together to try to resolve the problems they have. I do not think more hopper cars alone or additional and wider powers for the Wheat Board will completely resolve these problems.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I see we have ruffled the feathers of the Conservative chicken before he even starts debating.
The motion before the House today is very clear, and I want to point this out in response to my friend, the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley. It says clearly we want to add 4,000 hopper cars and 5,000 repaired boxcars to the grain fleet, and we want the railways to pay for this. He was criticizing the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre by saying that that hon. member wanted to give a handout to the railways by subsidizing the railways for the real cost of hauling grain; in other words, covering the difference between the Crowsnest pass rate and the real cost. What we are saying is that if they do not haul the grain, they will not get the money. The quid pro quo here is that if they get the money compensating them for hauling grain, they should damn well pay for hopper cars, repair the boxcars and meet all the other costs required for hauling grain. Railroads have been given sufficient subsidies over the years so that if they are making a decent buck hauling grain, they should darn well pay for the hopper cars and pay for repairing the boxcars needed to haul that grain.
Some Liberal members have asked us why all those boxcars. I just want to quote an article in the Leader Post in which officials of the Wheat Board themselves give us an idea what to say in the motion which is before us. This is an article dated July 22, 1978. At page 22 we find the following:
A spokesman for the Canadian Wheat Board in Winnipeg said the federal government has been told an additional 4,000 new hopper cars plus 5,000 rehabilitated boxcars are required to meet present grain movement needs.
Here is the Wheat Board saying they need these additional cars. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley thinks the opposition is often too negative. I agree that some of the speeches we heard from members on my right have been negative, but I think the speech made by the hon. member for

Regina-Lake Centre on the motion was very positive. We have a lot of respect for the Wheat Board, we think they are doing an excellent job, but we also think they need a few more tools with which to do a better job. One is the availability to them of a larger grain-moving fleet. That is what our motion is saying.
If hon. members want to find some other data, look at some of the concerns expressed by some of the commissioners of the Wheat Board about our recent sale to China. As hon. members know, we sold around three million metric tonnes to China. One of the Wheat Board commissioners told my friend, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, that if our grain had been moving efficiently, we could have sold about four million tonnes to China; and if it had been moving really efficiently, we could have sold six million tonnes to China. That is a really big order. It means a lot, not just to farmers, but in terms of Canada's balance of payments, in terms of our dollar, our economic activity and our unemployment situation, and in terms of all kinds of other things that are needed in this country.
We are having such a problem trying to balance those payments that a small investment in boxcars alone would help go a long way toward making our economy more healthy. Commissioner F. Hetland said that if we had some 4,000 extra hopper cars, we would have a net increase in sales of grain worth $700 million a year. That would even help Newfoundland, even though that province does not produce grain, because it would give stimulus to the economy, it would strengthen our dollar, it would create more jobs, it would help our balance of trade, and it would make Canada a much more attractive place economically of which all of us could be proud.
Let me go on to quote the chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board who was speaking at the same convention as that attended by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. I am referring to Mr. Esmond Jarvis. On November 9 he said that in the last year we had some $350 million worth of lost sales because of the deferred sales. They turned out to be a real loss to the Canadian economy, according to the chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board.
I think the motion before us today is a very sound one, a very positive and constructive motion. I notice the minister in charge of the Wheat Board himself is waffling on this. He said, if I remember correctly, that if this were last year, if we did not have the cutbacks that the heavies in the cabinet, such as the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde), had forced on the government, perhaps we would have already put in an order for more hopper cars. But because we have restraint in the government, the minister cannot make that argument forcefully enough at the cabinet table. So I am not sure precisely where the minister stands. He said clearly that there were two arguments. One is: yes, we need more hopper cars; the other argument is: no, we do not need them at this time.
In terms of the second part of the motion which gives to the Wheat Board total authority to co-ordinate grain movement in our country, our party is clear on this. We think all grains should be co-ordinated by one grains board which should have authority on behalf of the farmer. We are talking here about
November 13, 1978

total authority. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board said, if I remember correctly, that he thinks the Wheat Board could have that authority now under the legislation which is being passed through parliament. The minister is a lawyer and it seems strange to hear him say he thinks it might have that power. I should like to hear from him whether or not he really believes it does have that power, and if it does, is he willing to use it? Is he willing to give the Wheat Board power to co-ordinate grain movement in the country, which I know some of the commissioners want?
Those are the two main thrusts of the motion before us today. Now I want to present some arguments as to why I think this House should strongly endorse the position taken by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. I sincerely believe that the CPR in particular, and the railways in general, are on strike against Canadian farmers. Basically they are on strike because they want more money to haul grain. What they are receiving now is the amount guaranteed by the Crow rate. American companies receive approximately three or four times as much for hauling the same bushel of grain over an equivalent distance. This makes our railways very envious, so they continue to run down the service. They deplete services and do not repair boxcars. They put less and less money into the system until the government perhaps bails them out totally and completely. If that is not a strike against Canadian farmers, I do not know what a strike is.
We should use all the available precedents for legislating workers back to work, be they grain handlers, postal workers or any other group. We should legislate the CPR back to work. Under section 262 of the Railway Act, the government has the power to legislate the railways in this country back to work.
I want to illustrate what I really mean when I talk about the railways striking. Through its generosity, the government of Canada in the last few years has purchased 8,000 hopper cars to move farmers' grain. Because of that, many people think that Canada has more grain moving capacity now than prior to the purchase. Back in 1972 the CNR and CPR had 26,000 boxcars moving grain in Canada. In 1978 the number of boxcars was reduced to 12,800. That is a loss of approximately 13,200 boxcars. If one combines the 8,000 hopper cars and the 12,800 boxcars, one will find that Canada's grain moving capacity is less than it was before the hopper cars were purchased. Each hopper car is equivalent to 1.5 boxcars. Thus,
8,000	hopper cars equals approximately 12,000 boxcars. If that is added to the 12,800 boxcars which the railways have presently, one will find that there are 1,200 boxcars less than there were in 1972.

speechtext: There was more efficiency.

speechtext:
If it was for efficiency, I would be very, very pleased. I should like to tell the minister in charge of Canadian unity what he means by efficiency. The National Farmers Union, good friends of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, had an operation last year which was called "Car
Movement of Grain
Wars" or "Sky Spy". In operation "Sky Spy", they flew over approximately 6,000 miles of railway track in Canada to spy on the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board to see what he was doing about moving grain. They saw the efficiency which the minister in charge of the unity question is so concerned about. They found that hundreds of cars were sitting at delivery points for over a month after being filled but before being moved to the terminal. That is not efficiency. Also they found that thousands of CN and CP cars-I am not talking about hopper cars-had been on the sidings with "bad orders" forms, some as old as 1974.
I should like to refer to part of a brief which was released by the National Farmers Union a couple of months ago and reads as follows:
Our members found thousands of boxcars sitting on sidings or on abandoned lines with "bad order" forms on them. The state of disrepair was assessed by qualified railway engineers and in a substantial number of cases the cars have minimal damage. We have found bad orders forms dating from 1974. That means boxcars have been sitting idle for four years when a small investment on repairs could have put them back into service. Instead they are left abandoned and some cars have been badly vandalized. We have seen a bad order form dated 1975 which indicates the cars merely needed cleaning.
Further on in the brief it continues:
As you already know, we have found CN and CP boxcars in the U.S. hauling American grain. We found, on average, three Canadian cars for every mile of American track flown over. Recently 20 CN hopper cars were seen as far south as Fort Pierre in South Dakota close to the Nebraska border. CP is shipping American grain through Canada on the backaul to help American grain companies get their shipments through to the U.S. west coast ports.
I could refer repeatedly to the study made by the National Farmers Union.

speechtext: They ship American grain to Canada in Canadian cars.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Clearly the railways have gone on strike against ordinary Canadians and farmers. They are not repairing their boxcars, and they are being very inefficient about the manner in which cars are allocated. They are going on strike because the rail sectors of the CPR and CNR are not paying

November 13, 1978
Movement of Grain
very much in terms of profit, and they do not believe they are receiving enough for handling grain. As I said before, the railways in the United States receive three or four times as much for hauling a bushel of grain over the same number of miles.
We should legislate them back to work. We believe this can be done under the Railway Act, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) and I already have said. If the minister legislates them back to work, I guarantee the support of my party. They should be made to allocate a certain amount of their investment money and cash reserves to purchase hopper cars and to purchase and repair boxcars in order to move grain in the country.
The minister went part way this afternoon by indicating he will ensure that the CPR will repair its cars. I hope he really means that. I hope he uses a heavy fist with the CPR. I hope this is not just rhetoric but that he really means it.
As we have indicated in our motion, 1,000 boxcars are not good enough. Approximately 5,000 in this country require repair. The situation is serious. Some people have asked, "What does repairing a few boxcars really mean? Is the problem not really the production of grain, the over-production of it and the acquisition of more markets?" I should like to refer to my riding and the stockpile of grain in Canada.
Last week a little survey was conducted in my constituency, and we found that most of the elevators were plugged, there is a shortage of boxcars, and there is a lot of concern, as I am sure is the case in the Marquette constituency of Manitoba, about the situation because most of the grain goes through to Thunder Bay. Despite the fact the elevators are plugged, we have found out that there is space in Thunder Bay. That does not make very much sense.
One must keep in mind that in approximately three or four weeks the Thunder Bay route will be frozen due to weather conditions; if we do not move the grain to the terminals in Thunder Bay very quickly, it will be stuck for the winter; and that there are tremendous stockpiles of grain in the country. This year Canada will sell approximately 21 million tonnes of grain. Just a few years ago our biggest sales were 21.6 million tonnes of grain. The most recent estimates of the farm stocks by the Canadian Wheat Board show that we will sell this year 20.4 million tonnes of wheat, 3.3 tonnes of Durum, 1.8 million tonnes of oats, 8.7 million tonnes of barley, .63 million tonnes of rye, .65 million tonnes of flax and 3.7 million tonnes of rape, a total of 39.3 million tonnes. Because of the lack of grain handling facilities we are capable of handling only 21 million tonnes, approximately 50 per cent of the farm stocks.
The Wheat Board talks about the lack of boxcars and hopper cars and the damage it is causing to the Canadian economy. Not until 1985 are we expected to be capable of handling 35 million tonnes a year. This indicates the urgency of the debate before us today and, it is why we must insist that railways repair their boxcars and begin purchasing hopper cars and boxcars from their own funds.

speechtext:
I shall be finished, Mr. Speaker, in three or four minutes. I would like to remind the House that we have a deficit in our balance of payments this year of $4,150 million. If it was not for the tremendous surplus in wheat and barley sales, that deficit would be well over $6 billion because our sales last year were $2,273 million in those two grains. As Commissioner Hetland said, if we had 4,000 more hopper cars we would have another $700 million in grain sales every year. It is important that this House express very strongly to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and the railroads, the fact that we are serious about wanting them to repair their boxcars and about having them put more hopper cars on the rails for the farmers of this country.
There is a lot of concern in Saskatchewan that the off-board grain is eroding the superiority of the Canadian Wheat Board and hurting the quota system which is the basis by which farmers have an equal shot at hauling grain to the elevators. Many spokesmen in the west, such as the commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board and the head of the UGG, are concerned about this very thing. In fact, the only people who are not concerned about the off-board grain situation are the spokesmen for the Conservative party and for Cargill. I have a quote here from Cargill grain about the fact that the Wheat Board is getting tougher in off-board grain and, that they are getting very defensive because they are saying it will destroy competition in the wheat market.
I know that members of the Conservative party are the apologists for the open market, firms like Cargill and Continental. They want to abolish as well the Canadian Wheat Board. That party is the only party in this House that has really come clean and said that they would definitely like to do all these things. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board wants to be half pregnant because sometimes he is on the good side and, sometimes he is on the bad side, but you really never know where he stands. I admire the Conservative party for standing clearly on the side of firms like the Richardson Grain Exchange and the private grain enterprise in this country and for adopting the policies of the nineteenth century. In fact, the hon. member for Vegreville has boasted about barley on the open market and how great the situation is.
The Canadian livestock feed board in its weekly feed grain market report for the week ending October 25, says that the per tonne price of off-board barley was $75.80. If you look at Wheat Board barley, the price was $97.10, substantially higher. If all grain was sold through the Canadian Wheat Board, all Canadian farmers would get a much better price for their barley. However, this is not the philosophy of the Conservative party; their philosophy is to make sure that the grain is sold so that the speculators benefit and be damned the price the poor farmer gets.
November 13, 1978

I can recall the stories of my father and grandfather when the Canadian Wheat Board was formed in 1935. Then the price of a bushel of wheat was only a few pennies, but when it was sold in the spring, after the boys in the grain exchange had finished with it, it was being sold at well over $1 a bushel. They were overcharging the consumers, other nations around the world, and at the same time were parasites, living off the backs of farmers.
Those are the issues confronting us in this debate today. I am very pleased that the Conservative party has taken a clear position, as I said, in its support of the policies of the 19th century. I just hope that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board will get off the fence or fall off on the side of the Wheat Board, giving it more strength; and also that he will get really tough with the railways, as he is being with some of the working people in this country, so that they will do a job on behalf of the farmers and on behalf of each and every Canadian.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
