subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) is asking me what a bushel of grain looks like. Well, of course no grain is grown in the area of Quebec where I come from and also there is no railway system going through my area, but I can assure him however that the well-being of western farmers and the fact that the greatest possible number of bushels of grains are being moved on Canadian systems and exported is a blessing for the whole economy of this country as much for the constituents of my riding as the constituents of his riding.
Mr. Speaker, after listening today to the speeches made by hon. members on the other side of the House, an unaware listener could be led to believe that there is not an ounce of grain being moved at this time on railway systems in western Canada. Speeches like that, Mr. Speaker, can mislead not only this House but also all Canadians. Of course there are problems in the movement of grain, and we are aware of that; members must not only mention those problems but they should also be aware that this year as in past years more than 700 million bushels will be moved on those systems which members of the opposition consider inefficient and also as being the universal cause of the failure of grain transportation in Canada. There is no failure, Mr. Speaker, quite the contrary, there is a steady increase in the potential of that system. The motion introduced by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is important, and I believe it is essential to discuss the movement of grain as often as possible both in this House and other forums in Canada because it is one of the most important elements of the Canadian economy. And, Mr. Speaker, all Canadians must be aware that grain export is the major factor allowing us to maintain a steady balance of payments in Canada.
Movement of Grain
To improve the system, the mover asks or demands that railways, and I quote:
-add 4,000 hoppers cars and 5,000 repaired boxcars to their grain fleet;-
He also adds that the Canadian Wheat Board should have more authority. That might be a good suggestion, Mr. Speaker, but the hon. member carefully omitted to say what his request means in terms of dollars. He also omitted to put a timeframe on his request. And why did he avoid, Mr. Speaker, setting this timetable and quantifying the amount of money his demand can represent? Simply because the New Democratic Party is most likely a party which will never exercize the responsibility of taking real decisions in this country.
The other solution put forth by the New Democratic Party is to nationalize the Canadian Pacific.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext: It is a very good idea.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I confess that I feel some sympathy for this suggestion and that it may appear to be rather appealing solution in areas of Canada where the railway companies, either Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, have tried not to provide the necessary service for Canadians. However, I think that the middle of the way solution put forth by this government and those which preceded it and which consists in maintaining the powerful state owned network besides a privately owned network is probably the best solution. It is also important aggressively and efficiently with private networks such as Canadian Pacific in such a way that the latter will be compelled to follow the same course and provide the best possible service to the western farmers as well as all Canadians in the field of commodities transportation.
On the Tory side, Mr. Speaker, we have my colleague for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) who naturally deals very seriously with the issue of grain movement as with all the issues in the field of transportation in Canada, with great sincerity I am sure of it. He rightfully tries to find which solutions would be best to provide the best possible service to Canadians, be it in the field of grain movement or in other fields.
However the speeches delivered by my Progressive Conservative friends contain the same basic and unfortunately regular inconsistency of that party. On one hand they ask for additional or increased public funds to enable the railways to purchase their own hopper cars or improve their lines and they say to the government: "Give more money to the railway companies". However, on the other hand, for the sake of the sacrosanct free enterprise and competition they say: "Mind your own business, we have enough state intervention." Now, Mr. Speaker, I think that the inconsistency is apparent and with such a base for discussion, we cannot go very far.
Having briefly dealt with the comments of my colleagues opposite, let us see what the government has done and continues to do to improve the grain transport system. It is appropriate, Mr. Speaker, to remind the House that in 1973 the

November 13, 1978
Movement of Grain
government purchased 2,000 hopper cars. In 1974-75 we added 4,000 new hopper cars and in 1977 we added another
2,000.	In other words, Mr. Speaker, over the last five years the government gave to the grain transport system 8,000 hopper cars at an approximate cost of $260 million, and this is only one of many sides of the governmental action in this field.
Another aspect which is worth mentioning is the upgrading of rails. As the minister said this afternoon, and this was repeated by some of colleagues, it is good to know that last year the government invested $100 million to upgrade rails and that it plans to invest $70 million in similar works next year. Right now, Mr. Speaker, 50 per cent of the rail system in western Canada cannot accommodate these new hopper cars because they are too heavy for the existing rails. So, through this railroad upgrading program in which we already have invested $170 million and in which we have undertaken to invest more than $500 million in the coming years, I believe the improvement of the system will enable us to reach, in years to come, the target of one billion bushels of grain moved over that network, objective set for 1985, I think. It should be achieved easily.
Mr. Speaker, speaking now of another matter, namely increased storage of grains, I should like to quote the excellent reply given by my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), to the hon. member for Vegreville in the House last Thursday November 9; I quote from the Hansard for that day, on page 997. The parliamentary secretary was answering the hon. member for Vegreville. After having summed up our interventions with regard to hopper cars, our interventions in the field of railway line improvements, the parliamentary secretary said, and I quote:
The federal government has also contributed to the repair costs of several thousand box cars that will increase our capacity in the short term. Recent improvements to branch lines to Churchill under the prairies branch lines renovation program have also effectively increased our grain exportation capacity through that port.
We are also increasing the capacity of grain terminals in Canada. Under the storage improvement program of the Canadian Wheat Board, the storage capacity should improve by 40 per cent in Vancouver. Half of the storage capacity increase of 5.8 million tons must be done before the coming winter. The rest will be completed by the end of next year.
I should like to quote another paragraph where the parliamentary secretary says, as follow:
Major improvements are being made to increase our present and future export capacity.
We are now studying all possible means to transport a maximum quantity of grain through the St. Lawrence Seaway before its closing, including the extension of operating hours whenever possible. But we do not deal only with those urgent problems, Mr. Speaker, we are also concerned by problems that will be faced in the long term by our grain transportation and hauling system. We commissioned an inquiry, the Hall commission, on complex social and economic factors related to that system. We should soon establish in the prairies a

comprehensive basic branch line system that will be operated at least until the year 2000.
Mr. Speaker, an hon. member, the one for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) I think, was telling this afternoon that the grain hauling system out west had been studied to death. Yet it is surprising to note that at the first opportunity opposition members do not hesitate to refer to findings of the Hall commission to state that the government has not been up to its commitments, etc., whereas since the tabling of the commission's major recommendations the government has been busy acting with great celerity to protect immediately, and until the year 2000, all the lines recommended by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, those which should be part of the basic network of the prairie railway. Also concerning a second category of lines to be studied, jfiie government has acted very rapidly to protect the 2,344 miles of lines which were categorized as "uncertain" and it is expected that by the end of 1980 a decision will be made about those lines. It means, Mr. Speaker, that is in less than a year and a half from now western farmers and all users of the railway service of this region will be able to count on an improved system serviceable all year round.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members readily refer to the conclusions of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall's report, and in the past they used to refer also to another report, namely the Snavely Commission report. But by sheer accident, members opposite have refrained from referring to it because in its final report the Snavely commission states that Canadian products are arriving on export markets faster and in better condition than they have since many years. Of course, by all means our hon. friends opposite will avoid publicizing those positions, those extremely positive conclusions by the Snavely commission. Furthermore, the report indicates that the financial help of the federal government contributed to improve considerably the transportation system since the advisers of the Board have begun studying the cost structure in 1974.
The Snavely report also emphasizes that in 1947 only 9 per cent of grain cars were modern hopper cars whereas in 1977 the proportion was 30 per cent. In addition, more efficient planning enabled us to make better use of the cars since in 1977 an ordinary car made 3.3 more trips than in 1974. This shows that improvements to the system combined with the use of more powerful engines and better tracks reduced by one third the total number of cars which were necessary to transport the grain last year. The report also indicates a marked increase in grain markets in the ports of Vancouver and Churchill. In 1977, 34 per cent of the export business was made in Vancouver compared to 27 per cent in 1974. In Churchill, the export volume increased by 62 per cent between 1974 and 1977 and 3.6 per cent of the total of Canadian exports were handled there last year. Of course, all those conclusions are ignored by our colleagues opposite. And the name of the report, the name Snavely, has totally disappeared from their vocabulary since the publication of this document.
November 13, 1978

My colleague from Regina-Lake Centre says that Mr. Snavely is wrong, Mr. Speaker. I cannot, in tonight's debate, go into a long discussion with him on that issue, but I would be very happy to sit down with him and do so. Together we could review Mr. Snavely's conclusions which show, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that the variable costs of grain transport have risen from $247.1 million to $355.9 million in three years, which means an increase of only 13 per cent per ton. Producers' costs have also gone from $89.7 million to $114.8 million, a comparable increase. So, Mr. Speaker, there are not only negative sides to grain transport, and I think that the government can be proud of the action it has taken in this sector and of the improvements in rolling stock, ways and volume of grain export.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to come back to the importance of this issue for all Canadians. The importance that is recognized by this House and by the government points to one of the most significant facets of our Canadian federation. As I said, grain is one of the key positive factors in our Canadian economy, and grain exports account for some degree of equilibrium in our balance of payments. Quite understandably hon. members from the western provinces and governments of those grain producing provinces as well as farmers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are trying all they can to improve the movement of grain, their potential for larger and larger crops and more and better conditions for maximum revenues. It is quite understandable these concerns are expressed here at the national government level, just as the regional concerns of another province I am more familiar with, the province of Quebec, because we from Quebec have legitimate demands within this federation the same way as the western provinces, the Maritimes or British Columbia. Of course, we all have very strong regional concerns and therein lies the wisdom of our parliamentary system, under which we have a strong central government ensuring some balance between regional interests and a fair redistribution of wealth and interests between the various parts of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this important debate opened today by the motion put forward by my friend the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre gives me an opportunity to conclude on that vision of our country that is most important, namely the meeting of regional interests in central parliament where, side by side, whether opposition of government members, we have a duty to try and give Canadians across the country the best possible service, the fairest redistribution of wealth, and I rest assured that the hon. member put the motion forward in the best of spirits, and I would like to commend him for having shown such a spirit of generosity toward all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the chance to speak on the problems of the western grain industry made possible through the motion put by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) regarding hopper cars
Movement of Grain
provided by the Wheat Board. Being an ex-station agent he is no doubt an expert in this field. This is a problem we have had for a long time. In the issue of the Western Producer for October 26 the headline is: "Railways, Government blame each other for Grain Shortfalls". The article reads:
Railway company spokesmen and government officials pointed accusing fingers at one another when short-falls in the grain handling system were discussed at the Canada Grains Council semi-annual meeting here Oct. 18.
Spokesmen for Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways said they had sufficient capacity to move grain to export shipping positions if winter shipping surges were spread out over a 300-day shipping season.
I think this is of interest whatever private industry and nationalized industry have to say; they both get together when discussing grain at this time. On a more local level, I remember meeting a grain area supervisor in my riding a few years ago. I asked him, "How is the grain business?" He answered, "When the cars arrive and they are one week late-they are supposed to come on a Tuesday and they arrive on a Thursday-well, we eventually get things done, but sometimes it is rather difficult." We do not know whether the answer lies in more expenditures by the government out of treasury to buy hopper cars. We are not even sure they are being used to full advantage, even when they are under the control of the Wheat Board or the railroads, but this provides them with an opportunity to discuss their problems.
There is no doubt about the seriousness of the transportation problem, at least from an export point of view and the point of view of the good of the Canadian economy. Although sales are good, probably surprisingly good, the farmers have not been able to capitalize on the saleability of their products so that many elevators are congested. While we talk about record grain movement, in some grades such as No. 3 Utility wheat and No. 3 Red there has been little movement, at least in my riding, and the barley producers have been left with little opportunity to sell their grain unless it is to the local feed mill operator. There is practically nothing moving through the board.
It is small wonder that the farmer finds the movement of his grain curtailed or controlled by the Wheat Board. These grain handling companies are often farmer owned, but the farmer finds himself isolated and cut off from the management, all of whom issue contradictory statements and seem to be taking positions antagonistic to what he regards as his best interests. I would like to say that with this conflict of interest coming up, I am glad to have my chance of speaking as a permit holder. Grain is grown by some 200,000 permit holders. It is handled by a monopolistic Wheat Board supposedly working in the farmers' interest and by the railroads and other parts of the transportation system. In many cases the movement of grain seems stymied. Of course, there are government regulations covering the Wheat Board, the railways and the grains commission. Many of these seem to have the effect of limiting the movement of the farmers' grain.
In a general way, I am not in favour of the government of Canada purchasing hopper cars for the use of the railway and

November 13, 1978
Movement of Grain
the grain-handling system, at least without considerable strings attached. As a starter, hopper cars may have seemed a more feasible method of transporting grain than boxcars.
Why are hopper cars not purchased by the railways directly, or even better, by the grain handling companies? Railways purchase their own rolling stock. I understand the oil companies have found it to their advantage to own, manage and route their own cars. If the grain handling companies were charged with moving the grain under their jurisdiction, with the Wheat Board giving them a target to move, they would do better than at present. This possibility deserves to be carefully investigated.
Much better use apparently is made of cars as far as oil companies are concerned when they are owned or at least leased by the oil company. Unfortunately, the manufacture of hopper cars is being directed by the government into areas of high unemployment, and to some extent they represent an unemployment measure rather than their primary purpose of providing service to the western grain producer.
The western grain transportation system is approaching the limit of chaos and recriminations fly thick and fast. The Wheat Board has implied that the railroads are not pulling their weight and in this regard, for once, the railroads have fought back. Both the privately owned CPR and the publicly owned CNR say that their facilities are not being used in a proper manner and that they could haul much more grain if orders were placed in a rational way. Merely increasing the number of hopper cars to sit around deserted sidings or hidden away in isolated gravel spurs is not a particularly good way of moving the grain.
Either the railroads or the grain handling companies should provide the hopper cars or other means of transportation necessary for the movement of grain. Merely the government producing hopper cars is not enough. If the government does pay for the building of those cars, they should be leased to the railways. I understand there is no assessment as to the cost of these hopper cars and no method to provide for their upkeep.
Recently in my constituency there was a shortage of boxcars or hopper cars. It was found they were available, but there were no work crews and no power to haul the cars because of cutbacks and other activities of the railroads which had sopped up their working force. In my constituency, the CNR is the only railway of any consequence.
Obviously one of the important things to consider is who should supply the hopper cars, who should pay their initial cost and who should control them. Should it be the Wheat Board or the grain handling companies? Should producers have the right to order cars? Under the new order of the past few weeks, it seems that right will be taken away from producers or at least be restricted. That right seems to be challenged by the Wheat Board. The producers have fought for these rights over the years. They have fought to order their own cars. At the moment, this right is being jeopardized. It is being challenged by the Wheat Board on the basis that it must control the movement of grain. This is an important principle to consider.
In other words, should we become more and more bureaucratic, controlling the movement of grain in a bureaucratic way, which the NDP would like, or attempt to free it in order to provide a degree of competition that does not seem to prevail at the moment?
Overriding all that, of course, is the problem of the Crows-nest rates. It is now generally realized that it is not practical for the railroads to haul grain at the rates set out in the Crow rates and maintain a viable rail operation. For many years the railways have complained they have not been making money. It seems that the Crowsnest rates were not unreasonable until the last three or four years. While their costs increased, their efficiency increased as well. Therefore, four or five years ago they were still in the black with regard to hauling grain.
Railways are becoming an increasingly expensive operation. Wage structures have continued to rise along with those in other parts of industry. The price of grain at the moment is low. Indeed, in many respects it approaches the low levels of the depression years. It is perhaps fair to say that a grain grower with a section of land might gross $30,000 a year in returns and, after his expenses and a modest return to himself and his living costs are taken out, there is certainly not much left. Can he afford to have his grain hauled down the track by a railroad whose wage structure is much greater than his own? Can he afford to have his grain hauled down the Great Lakes by engineers who earn much more than he would hope to make out of his crop? This gives us considerable food for thought. I would calculate that if present prices in the grain industry are projected, they would probably return something like $3 to $4 an hour for a farmer's work. It certainly puts him in at the lower end of the scale.
The question arises, can the farmer reduce his dependency on the grain handling system and can he profitably take over some of the grain handling transportation that has hitherto been reserved for the railroads? The grain handling system was built for the horse and wagon and elevator points were situated accordingly. But grain hauls of 40 to 50 miles are now common, and as roads improve, highways open up and farms get bigger, transportation is made available. It certainly seems possible that farmers who invest $50,000 or $60,000 in a combine or a tractor would not be able to invest similar prices in a truck to haul their grain to more central gathering points. A haul of 50 or 60 miles may not seem much when the grain is destined for Thunder Bay, a distance of 700 to 800 miles. However, if a producer lives on a branch line, a haul of 50 to 60 miles may well mean that the grain, from an economic point of view, has been hauled half way to Thunder Bay. The farmer's costs may not have been so much out of line with what it costs the railway to maintain a short branch and the attendant large number of people involved in merely standby operations to maintain services.
Construction in the grain transportation system is having some important effects. It seems that with longer hauls by farmers and reduced quotas they have to turn more and more to crops that produce a large amount of money per bushel. Therefore, in areas that are suitable, special crops are receiv-

November 13, 1978

ing more and more attention. The growing of oats has practically ceased, except for local use, as they are pretty well defeated by the high cost of tranportation. Barley is fast approaching the same point and there may well be a reduction in the amount of barley produced if this congestion increases or, conversely, barley will be fed at a local level. We may also be faced with increased pork production.
1 I now wish to refer to the off-board quota. This has become a bone of contention. In fact, if there had not been off-board quotas, many farmers in my area would have delivered no wheat or barley this past season. For instance, we have quotas of, say, five bushels for wheat. But five bushels of No. 1 and five bushels of utility wheat mean a great deal of difference in dollars, because No. 1 brings twice the amount per acre as No. 3 utility, yet for many farmers there was only No. 3 utility wheat last year. Again this year most of the crop seems to be No. 3 red or No. 3 utility. In fact, there was practically no movement of No. 3 utility out of my riding last year. The Wheat Board could not seem to find any sales for it, they said. Without off-board quotas, it does not seem likely any would have moved.
Perhaps this situation will change but the Wheat Board will have to show that it can move the grain. As I understand it, the Montreal feed market is the place where most of the off-board grain is going, so presumably if there are no off-board quotas Wheat Board sales to that market would increase. But there feed grains are in competition with American corn, and in many practical ways it is easier to obtain American corn in the eastern market than western feed grains. A good many farmers have been able to sell grain whereas without the off-board quotas they would have had no market whatsoever and would have been reduced to selling at the local level if they could find any buyers.
It is some years since there has been a glut of feed grains on the prairies, and since then agriculture has changed a lot. There seems less possibility of a greater food-producing industry developing than was the case seven or eight years ago. There are fewer people on the farms and they are not of an age group to be able to involve themselves in the feeding of pigs, always the main meat raised when there is a surplus of feed grains. So the problem becomes relatively greater than it was eight or ten years ago.
Then what about the selling of No. 3 red under the quota system? I am thinking particularly of the Parkland area. It seems likely that with the change in the grading system we shall rarely produce anything more than No. 3 red wheat, at least half of the time anyway. It seems the best the farmers in the Parkland area can get is No. 2 red; with the first shower it is down to No. 3 red and with the second shower it is into the No. 3 utility grade.
The Wheat Board does not seem to be able to move this grain and perhaps I can understand some of the reasons. After all, No. 1 and No. 2 grades bring much more in the way of price, and it costs no more to move than a bushel of No. 3
Movement of Grain
utility. As they bring a dollar or two more a bushel, I can understand the desire of the board to move them. But is this the fairest way of doing things? Should the board be put in the position where it must ration available sales? And what about the barley growers? They are even further down the ladder than the utility wheat people because their grain is less saleable. These are some of the problems which have to be addressed, particularly in the northern parts of the prairie wheat growing area.
I would like to end with one problem of the grain industry which should be set at rest once and for all, and it is this. Does the government intend to put into effect the restricted hours of work for elevator agents? The minister in charge of the Wheat Board is quoted in the Winnipeg papers as telling the Manitoba Wheat Pool that there will be an indefinite suspension of the so-called 40 and eight hours of work by country elevator agents. I think this is important because a great deal of rationalization, a great deal of the future of the country elevator system, is bound up with this apparently simple question. In the elevator system it is a very important factor, and while the minister perhaps does not have full authority to make an announcement, I hope he will prevail on the Acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet) to make this announcement in the very near future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard today from non-farmers and retired station agents. I would like to put my two-cents worth in as a member of parliament from an area which has the only inland port in central Canada.
The present government's blatant inability to program grain shipments has cost Canada an additional 4 million tonnes in foreign grain sales and a deferment of 1.5 million tonnes for delivery in 1979. Our grain transportation system is choked by a tremendous backlog in deliveries that has delayed grain shipments right from the start of the 1978 shipping season this spring. Following three record crops, producers have stocks overflowing their on-farm facilities. Prairie grain elevators are stuffed, holding 35 per cent more stock than a year ago, yet deliveries to these primary elevators are lagging behind 1977 figures. At the same time grain stocks at the major export terminals are down 33 per cent from last year. The problem is rail movement of grain to export positions, and more specifically, the scheduling of deliveries.
In this debate on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), I am speaking on behalf of the port of Churchill as well as the hinterland to the port of Churchill, which covers most of Saskatchewan where there are at least 118 million bushels of grain which could be destined for shipment through Churchill.
Instead of increasing our grain exports and developing new markets, Canada is losing her traditional customers. Foreign requests to purchase Canadian grain are being turned down because of this government's lack of foresight and initiative to update our transportation system to meet even present demands.

November 13, 1978
Movement of Grain
Our national deficit could be lowered significantly. Instead, grain handling facilities from country elevator to the port terminal limit us to 21 million tonnes of grain exports annually. And as far as this government is concerned, that is all they will supply.
This anomaly in government policy is best exemplified by the port of Churchill. This Manitoba port provides western producers a 10 per cent to 14 per cent higher net return, yet the government refuses to direct more than a nominal shipment of grain through the port. Grain shipments for the 1978 season through Churchill totalled 23 million bushels-down nine million bushels from the expected 32-million bushel quota.
Since only 23 million bushels have been shipped through the port, the port is in a cash loss position. This means that the deficit will have to be picked up by the taxpayers of Canada. Had the port been allocated a few million bushels more, its accounts would have been in the black, and there are not too many ports in Canada which find themselves in the black at year end.
The port of Churchill has a storage capacity of about four million bushels. A few years ago this facility had to be used for grain storage, but for some reason this government takes the approach that it is not going to store grain at Churchill. One of the excuses is that the government does not know just what grain sales it will have next year through that port. However, in this particular year there have already been cargoes sold for shipment next year through the port of Churchill. I therefore see no reason why-with this huge capacity-grain could not be moved into place.
This motion is before us today because there is a shortage of boxcars. It is my understanding that even if boxcars were made available at some later date, the port of Churchill would have to be opened during the winter, which might not be too acceptable. If cars could have been available this fall, the four million bushels could have been put into place before the ice and snow came. It is time the minister took off his blinkers and lifted his eyes to the north.
One-tenth of Canada's total grain exports moves through the port of Churchill. A senior economist for the Wheat Board, Harold F. Bjarnsson, has said that in just six years-by 1985-Canada should be able to export 20 million tonnes of wheat, up to 10 million tonnes of barley and 1.5 million tonnes of oilseeds, for a total of 31.5 million tonnes. That is an increase of 10.5 million tonnes, which will call for a 50 per cent increase in transportation and grain-handling facilities.
The port of Churchill can play a large role in the expansion of Canada's grain export industry. The Hall commission recommended an increase in grain shipments through Churchill to 55 million bushels, but to date this government can see its way clear to allow only a two million bushel per year increase in shipments. With the loss of some nine million bushels this year, it will take us up to five years to make that amount up.
Moreover, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has virtually ignored the Hall recommendations and commissioned a

second study, the Bryden report, to which I have referred before and which views further development as uneconomic. Now we are waiting for the results of a third report on grain handling and transportation. This government claims to be fighting for a strong federation, but until it can envision Canada as stretching north and south as well as east and west, it cannot hope to maintain a unified and prosperous country.
This year it was expected that the m.v. Arctic would be going to Churchill for a cargo of grain on November 15. I asked if the minister would consider also sending in or having three or four other ships accompany the m.v. Arctic, which is a class two icebreaker. In his reply the minister said he did not think that would be a feasible operation and that no one would want to send ships iri there.
That is not the kind of approach I would like to see taken. I think the minister should have pursued this matter in order to get at least another four million or five million bushels of grain out through the port of Churchill. Because the nine million bushel shortfall at Churchill will have to be made up through Prince Rupert and Vancouver this winter, and looking at the track record of grain handling facilities in this country, I am sure we will end up having that nine million bushels still sitting there next spring.
When I mentioned the m.v. Arctic, the minister said that it had encountered bad ice conditions and that a hole had been ripped in its side. The minister was clouding the issue for the simple reason that at that time the m.v. Arctic was coming from the Nanisivik Mines with a load of ore and it was out on the other side of Baffin Island in Baffin Bay. It was nowhere close to the shipping routes out of Churchill. It was on October 20 that the minister brought to the attention of the House that the m.v. Arctic had encountered ice. The last ship clearing Churchill this year did so on October 24 and encountered no problems whatsoever. I just wanted to clear that up.
The minister was saying that the m.v. Arctic was going to be scheduled for Churchill for November 15. It could not go there because of damage. I understand that it has to go to Rotterdam for complete repair. Because of the slow movement of grain in Canada, 1 ask the government to schedule the m.v. Arctic to go to Churchill by at least July 1, 1979 and to provide at least four or five ships to accompany the icebreaker to Churchill. Let us get the season started so that we can handle not only the anticipated 30 million or 32 million bushels out of Churchill but also set our goal a little higher than that.
I speak for grain handlers and those who work for the National Harbours Board in Churchill. Some of those fellows have lived there for 25 or 27 years, and it is a personal challenge for them to be able to reach and better what they reached in previous years. We have to have a commitment from the government. The minister must work with the Wheat Board, convince it that the CNR can get grain to Churchill and that ships can be scheduled to handle grain through that port.
One other concern to me regarding the port of Churchill also involves the ports of Montreal and Halifax. It is my
November 13, 1978

understanding that an in-house National Harbours Board task force has just been struck to examine the prospects of leasing the ports of Churchill, Montreal and Halifax. I do not know what the idea behind this is. I have not seen the terms of reference. Perhaps the government wants to lease these ports, for example, to Cargill, which would then be responsible for the ports. However, tied to that there would have to be some commitment that Cargill would have the necessary cars to move grain to those ports and thus increase the flow of grain. I look forward to the report of the task force, which is supposed to be released in two months.
The government and the Canadian Wheat Board must think of transportation of grain in this country on a north-south basis as well as on an east-west basis. The old east-west concept which was born at the time of confederation is just not sufficient to handle the amount of grain we are producing in Canada now. We are going to have to use the port of Churchill. When the government is replaced, and I do not think will be too long, 1 am sure the port of Churchill will be used to its maximum capacity in order to relieve the situation on the prairies and get grain moving.
We talk of boxcars' not being available. The distance from Saskatchewan to the port of Churchill is only half the distance from Saskatchewan to Thunder Bay, and it is a little further to Prince Rupert. We must use the port of Churchill so that we can move grain quicker. That is a commitment our party will make to the farmers and producers of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS IN MOVEMENT OF GRAIN FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of closing the debate on this major problem which exists in western Canada.
I should say at the outset that history is repeating itself. There is no doubt that today we are going through almost the same thing that grain producers went through 22 years ago. At that time grain was piling up on the prairies and the government of the day was not doing anything about it. It was defeated first in 1957 and then completely defeated in 1958. I see the same thing happening now when I witness the so-called experts on the government side ganging up together with the NDP against the Conservatives. This shows their tunnel vision. They do not realize what the problem is. It is very simple: get out and sell the grain that is there. If you sell it, you move it. These are the two simple things that need to be done.
This is what happened in 1960 and 1961. Hon. members opposite should realize that the then minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), made a trip to China at that time. One would have thought the world was coming to an end when those sales were made, and the NDP together with the Liberals of the day criticized those sales bitterly. Now they are following that example.
There is no doubt in my mind that the government will not be in a position to win the next election and that we will have the opportunity to move this grain, because it has to be moved. You can blame whom you like, the government, the railroads
Movement of Grain
or the Wheat Board. Nevertheless, the real crux of the problem is, first of all, to go out into the world market and sell it. We are competing now with other countries for grain sales because of the fact that there is a small surplus.
I am particularly concerned about some of the comments made by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) when he said that the western grain grower has fewer problems now than he had eight or ten years ago. He went on to say that if you compare the western grain farmer's net worth now with his net worth a number of years ago, you would find it is a lot greater. It is not the net worth that is important because many cemeteries are full of rich farmers. It is the net income that is important, and this is what members opposite do not seem to realize. The grain farmer must have an increase in profit so as to stay in business.
As much as I do not like statistics, I think I will have to put some on the record to set it straight. In the last five years, if we compare the cost of wheat with the increased cost of production, we find that it would have to sell at approximately $3.62 a bushel. What is it selling at? It is selling at $3.19 a bushel. This means that the western grain producer is falling behind and his costs are increasing tremendously. In the last 27 years the cost of machinery alone has gone up over 100 per cent.
I should like to impress upon members of the House that 30 years ago this fall feed grain in western Canada was selling at exactly the same price as it is this year. How in the world can anyone survive in that kind of situation, with increased cost of production, increased taxes, increased cost of fertilizer? That is why it is so urgent that the government realize the predicament of the grain farmer. Many grain farmers are going further into debt. The farm debt in western Canada has doubled in the last five years. This means added cost in interest. We have seen the cost of borrowing money go up in the last several months. The bank rate has increased six times this year. This is reflected in the cost of operation of the western grain farmer.
We cannot fool around with this situation because it is too important to our economic well-being, too important to those who are involved. Let me show exactly what is happening. I wish the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, his parliamentary secretary or anybody else on the other side would come over here so that I could show him a picture of farmers loading their own grain on their own cars. They have to go back to doing that because the elevators are plugged. This year alone 1,042 producer cars have been loaded between the beginning of the crop year, that is August 1, and the end of October. This compares with 250 producer cars shipped in the same period last year.
This proves the agility and versatility of the western grain producer, but let me impress upon members that he can only go so far; he can only spread himself so thin. If hon. members opposite, in the short time they have left on the government side of the House, do not do something about this, I can assure them that they, together with the NDP, if the latter continue to support the government, will not find any of their members
1086

November 13, 1978
Adjournment Debate
elected in any of the western provinces in the next election, and I would be prepared to wager that with any of them.
There has been a great deal of discussion with regard to the problems associated with the Crowsnest pass rate. I have to impress upon hon. members opposite and on the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, who is also the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), that problems in western Canada connected with the movement and sale of grain have created a schism between beef producers and grain producers. The government, the minister or the cabinet-I do not care who- are the logical people to get busy and alleviate this serious problem.
I hope that as a result of this debate the minister has become cognizant of the serious problem which exists on the prairies, because I have a great fear that hon. members opposite, who have never had to rely on net income from grain to pay for their groceries, to pay their bills or to maintain their families, do not realize the seriousness of this situation. I cannot express more firmly that it is very important that action be taken now.
Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate it if somebody on the other side of the House would let us know what the business is for tomorrow. Perhaps the government whip might be able to inform us.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will deal, in the following order, with Bill C-7, Bill C-5, and Bill C-10, whether or not we get to the final one. That is the order in which the government will put forward the business tomorrow.

subtopic: FLOODS-FLOOD PREVENTION PROGRAM IN NORTH MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
FLOODS-FLOOD PREVENTION PROGRAM IN NORTH MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I thank you for giving me this opportunity to rise once again on an issue which

has been the subject of several interventions not only from myself but also from the hon. member who took the floor before me as the representative of Laval riding, our good friend and colleague, Mr. Jean Rochon. It concerns the flood problem. We have been informed of the budget cuts made by the Government of Canada, and I think we all agree that budgets must be seriously trimmed down, but when we are directly concerned we may not agree so readily. So to lessen the effects of those budget cuts, considering the seriousness and the priority of our problem, floods in the Montreal area, I communicated with the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) last October 16 in a letter referring to the agreement made on October 4, 1976 between the Government of Canada and the government of Quebec whereby $5 million were to be earmarked for undertaking works in the Montreal region to reduce damages due to floods.
In August 1977, having examined together the situation, the two government levels agreed to extend the agreement for two years, in other words until March 31, 1980 and the Minister of State (Environment) confirmed that agreement to the Quebec natural resources minister on October 31, 1977. I expressed my concern over the possibility that this budget might be cut due to restraint measures.
I mentioned that I wanted to advise him that a cut would be hardly acceptable to people who live on the shore of the Prairies and Mille-Isles rivers and who must suffer those floods every spring time since almost 30 years. To make the public aware of that situation, all we have to do is to make them read again newspaper reports from 1963-64 and 1971. And now that almost everybody has a television, it is even easier to witness it through images.
Given the importance of those works, I asked a question of the minister last November 7. I asked him if he intended to cut expenses regarding the commitment I referred to earlier, and I learned that the release had been issued by some PQ members coming from that area who had mentioned that we were refusing to go ahead with our commitment before 1980. In his answer, the minister referred to an agreement of 1975.
I have with me a press release mentioning the implementation of a diking program in accordance with an agreement on hydrometrical survey cost sharing which was reached on March 17, 1975 between the Liberal government of Quebec represented by then minister Gilles Masse and the Canadian government. I was not completely satisfied with the minister's answer because it seemed to me that we did not directly tackle the problem I had raised. However I was a bit more optimistic when the minister told me that he would be on the site last Friday. The minister was given the opportunity to fly over the concrete dike built along the river to control the water level and also over the pumping station system established with a view to draining the water which could cause damage in spite of the dikes. I am optimistic about the minister's attitude but I am still concerned with the situation.
November 13, 1978

I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we put this question on top of our priorities in view of the damages that have been caused by spring floods in 1974. I refer here to a document issued by the department stating that the cost incurred by the Canadian government for damages caused by floods in the Ottawa River, the Mille-Isles River, Bizard Island and the Prairies River amounted to about $25.5 million for 1974 alone. It seems to me as was stated in the agreement, half of this amount would be sufficient to avoid any additional spending and that it would contribute considerably to improve a situation which has already lasted for too long.
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned this problem to make my colleagues in the House aware of the importance of this situation. The time allotted to me is limited but it seems to me we should give consideration to the natural resource contained in these two rivers, the Prairies River and the Mille-Isles River. This touristic attraction, this holiday attraction should not be a polluting factor, this natural resource should become as soon as possible a regional waterway centre, by the development of the Prairies and the Mille-Isles rivers and thus contribute to economic progress of the area north of Montreal. So it seems to me the provincial, municipal and federal governments should join hands in the pursuit of this goal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Pearsall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FLOODS-FLOOD PREVENTION PROGRAM IN NORTH MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of flooding in the Montreal area in the early 1970s the federal government, in full and equal partnership with the province of Quebec, conducted a comprehensive study of the causes of flooding and developed an integrated plan to remedy the problem. This plan included needed liaison with the bodies responsible for regulating the Great Lakes and in particular the flows in the St. Lawrence River. Schemes were mapped out to enlarge storage capacity in the upper part of the Ottawa basin and to provide for local diking and for control works at the head of the Mille Isles River, the most northerly outlet of Lake of Two Mountains. The integrated plan also included flood risk mapping.
The plan of which I speak was prepared by a federal-provincial committee in 1976. In October of that same year, implementation of its recommendations began. Since then, diking has been completed for three of the communities most severely affected and work should commence soon to protect a fourth community recommended as part of the integrated plan. Mapping of the flood risk areas in the Montreal region at a scale of 1 to 10,000 is complete, and a series of 22 maps is available to ensure that people know where the flood risk is greatest.
On May 11 of this year, the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) and the responsible provincial minister jointly designated the flood risk area, thereby assuring that the provincial and federal as well as local governments would discourage development in those areas, development that would be liable to future flooding. All the work that has been
Adjournment Debate
done to date has been done under formal agreement with Quebec, and this includes the studies, the mapping and the diking.
There are a number of communities in the Montreal region which remain unprotected, and discussions have been held with provincial authorities on this problem. Obviously, not all communities can receive protection at the same time, but our record in the Montreal region is one that the federal government can be proud of. Anyone implying anything else just does not understand the complexity of the flooding problem. As I stated earlier, we cannot work everywhere at once.
Flood control is extremely expensive and there are often alternative ways to provide protection. I have already mentioned the use of a storage reservoir in the upper basin and of control works at the upper end of the Mille Isles River. These alternatives to local protective works such as dikes can be just as effective. We-and I speak here of the federal government in conjunction with the province-have not completed all the work we have in the Montreal region; because of the cutbacks, the job will take longer than we previously thought. In the interim, studies are continuing jointly with both Quebec and Ontario on the best way to use the storage capacity of existing reservoirs, and of Lake Ontario, to reduce flooding in the Montreal region.

subtopic: FISHERIES-CLOSING OF ST. LAWRENCE, NEWFOUNDLAND FLUORSPAR MINE-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT IN INDUSTRY

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: FISHERIES-CLOSING OF ST. LAWRENCE, NEWFOUNDLAND FLUORSPAR MINE-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT IN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the town of St. Lawrence, Newfoundland, was sentenced to death by Alcan when they decided to close their fluorspar mining operation at St. Lawrence. The provincial government of Newfoundland together with Fishery Products Ltd. devised a scheme together with the local citizens' committee in St. Lawrence to resuscitate the town economically by constructing a fish plant in St. Lawrence, which has a fine harbour, and providing employment in the fish plant for the fishermen in that area who were formerly miners. Everything has been done, everyone is ready to go ahead except the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), who is dragging his feet, who has been delaying for some three months the decision whether or not two Portuguese gill-netting draggers can be permitted to fish into this plant and land their catch there so that there will be enough fish to keep the plant operating a reasonable length of the year to make it economic and viable.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the situation we are in now is that our fisheries dictator is dithering while the town of St. Lawrence is withering. The people are on unemployment insurance there and their unemployment insurance is starting to run out.
All arrangements were made for construction to start on this plant on August 1. It has been held up because we are waiting
8006S-69V2

November 13, 1978
Adjournment Debate
for the Minister of Fisheries of Canada. It is now November 13. The project is going to be supported by DREE. Fishery Products Ltd. is putting up its own money and there is a contribution from the provincial government.
Last January 20, a DREE assistant, Mr. Tom Webb, was quoted as saying that the federal government was a long way from making any decision on the proposed fish plant. Here we are eleven months later and there is still no decision on it. A spokesman in the minister's office on the same date, January 20, was non-committal when asked to predict the future date for a federal decision on the St. Lawrence proposal. He might well be non-committal. All the work has been done and in July, when the minister thought a general election was imminent, he gave general approval to the scheme.
Landed immigrant status was to be granted to Captain Almeida, the Portuguese owner, and his crews. The proposal was that the vessels would operate under a Canadian company. The fishermen would be landed immigrants and teach Newfoundlanders their techniques. Apparently, these vessels are really excellent and with their new methods, they catch a lot of fish. The Portuguese government objected to that method, however, and now the proposal has been before the minister for several months that there be a charter arrangement for these vessels so that they can land their fish under contract to this new fish plant in St. Lawrence. But still the minister does not act.
Today he said he was going to send a changed proposal to Fishery Products Ltd. this week. This means there will be no construction. It will not be ready in the spring. It will not be ready to receive fish next year. People will be coming off unemployment insurance and going on welfare, degraded, because of the lack of action by this minister.
This minister stopped the Nordsee investment in Harbour Grace that would have provided year round employment there. He is against any foreign control, any foreign entry into the fishery in Canada, but he has agreed to all kinds of deals with the Bulgarians and Russians for buying fish from the union in Newfoundland. He has agreed to East German trawlers landing fish at the lake plants on the south coast of Newfoundland-Canadian quota fish for the lake plants. He has agreed with Norwegian vessels landing fish at four fish plants at Conception Bay and one in Trinity Bay, but he will not agree to or make up his mind about this arrangement with two Portuguese vessels so that this new fish plant can be built in St. Lawrence to give those abandoned miners some hope for the future, some employment, some occupation to go back to. Why is it, Mr. Speaker, that the minister is carrying on like this?
It has been stated by the provincial government, by Fishery Products Ltd., by everyone involved, that the only thing holding this plant up now is the minister. I should like to put on the record some quotations from a column entitled "Double 007 Seven" which appeared in the Daily News on November 8. This column is usually very favourable to the minister and to the Liberal party. It reads in part as follows:

Unfortunately Ottawa, in the person of the Minister of Fisheries, Romeo LeBlanc, is being something less than co-operative.
In July, when a federal election appeared imminent, he quickly agreed to the proposal which included the use of two Portuguese-owned vessels to supplement locally caught fish and thus ensure a year-round production at the proposed plant.	.
A little later this statement appears:
His procrastination has prevented a goodly number of St. Lawrence men from obtaining work on the project during the winter months.
And still later the writer had this to say:
Either Mr. LeBlanc is completely heartless, excessively stupid, or someone had failed to inform him of the plight of the nearly three thousand people in the town.
The writer goes on to mention that their only hope is the member for the district, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). I say, where has the Secretary of State for External Affairs been while this affair has been going on, while this hang-up has been in effect since last August, while St. Lawrence is abandoned, while this fish plant has been stopped? Where is the Secretary of State for External Affairs? Is he going to be dictated to by the Minister of Fisheries who will not move, who is incapable of making up his mind-who only makes his mind up when the president of the fisheries union in Newfoundland, Richard Cashin, tells him to make it up? When is the Secretary of State for External Affairs going to make the Minister of Fisheries move on this matter which is preventing the fish plant from starting production down in St. Lawrence?
The new play is no longer "Waiting for Godot"; the new play is "Waiting for Romeo". There is decision after decision in his department waiting for him to make up his mind on. He has a pathological disdain for anything to do with countries outside of the Iron Curtain apparently. It is all right for East Germans to go and land their fish at lake plants on the south coast under an arrangement, but not for Portuguese to land fish at the town of St. Lawrence on the south coast. It is all right for Bulgarians and Russians too. It is all right for Poles. There is a deal that has been negotiated now with Poles for winter fish, but for some reason when it comes to the West Germans, Portuguese or whatever, he is incapable of making up his mind.
Captain Almeida and his two ships cannot control the fishery of Newfoundland; they cannot control this fish plant. The fish plant is going to be owned by Fishery Products Ltd., fully owned by them. These vessels will come under Canadian control. There is a simple chartering agreement that is put before the minister. He has agreed to charters for all of these other vessels I have mentioned. What is holding them up in agreeing to the chartering arrangements so that construction can start on this fish plant? It is now November 13 and it is unlikely that construction can even be started and be finished for next spring. They are going to lose their whole year's fishing in St. Lawrence. They will lose a year's employment. They will have to go on welfare. These are the people who have been laid off because the fluorspar mine closed down.
November 13, 1978

If the minister can give us some reasonable explanation, Mr. Speaker, we would be pleased to have it. But until we get it, we have to tell the minister that it is time for him to stop dithering and take action on this very serious problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Pearsall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-CLOSING OF ST. LAWRENCE, NEWFOUNDLAND FLUORSPAR MINE-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT IN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one is more anxious to solve the unemployment problem in the community of St. Lawrence than the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc). This is evidenced by the fact that the minister approved two licences for Fishery Products Ltd. and so advised the company on May 3 of this year. If the company had stuck to this original agreement we would have been able to provide the needed jobs for the community, and at the same time maintained control of fishing licences in the hands of Canadians.
However, this company was not able to stick to the agreed approach. They informed the department on August 15 of this year that they could not carry out the terms of the original proposal. The department immediately exchanged letters with the company and met with their principal officers in Montreal on October 3 in order to try and reach a mutually satisfactory solution. The terms the company was now proposing were considerably different from what they had agreed to earlier. In essence, the new proposal involved foreign ownership of the licences and this is unacceptable to the government and unacceptable to those Canadians in whose name we fought for the 200-mile zone.
The minister informed the House today-and I can only reaffirm it again tonight on his behalf-that the government will be making another proposal to the company which will allow them to proceed with the fish plant and, as a consequence, to supply the much needed employment for this community. The proposal should be made in a matter of days, and certainly no later than the end of this week. It is the minister's hope that the company will be able to proceed with the government's second offer when it is finalized. This offer, like the first, is consistent with the over-all policy for a controlled expansion of the fisheries, with control remaining in the hands of Canadians.
The Minister of Fisheries also assured the House that if the second proposal was unacceptable to Fishery Products Ltd., then other avenues would be quickly explored. In short, the minister has asked me again to assure the people of St. Lawrence that something will be done for them, and done by 1979.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT HAS SPECIAL ECONOMIC PROGRAM FOR NEWFOUNDLAND
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT HAS SPECIAL ECONOMIC PROGRAM FOR NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments this evening concern a special economic program for the province of Newfoundland in view of the high unemployment in Newfoundland and the sluggish performance of the economy, especially this year. I addressed a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) on October 30, 1978 to that effect and the minister answered by saying that consideration is always given to parts of the
Adjournment Debate
country like Newfoundland. He cited the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and government employment programs such as Canada Works as ways in which the federal government helps. Although DREE and the work programs have been in effect for many years in the province of Newfoundland, we still have a depression level of unemployment.
These programs of the federal government do not get at the root causes of unemployment in Newfoundland. The root causes are not served by these federal programs. Unemployment in Newfoundland is directly related to the province's position with the rest of Canada. A good example of how its position with the rest of Canada has a detrimental effect with regard to government programs was the 3 per cent remission of sales tax enacted by the federal government last spring. It was of little benefit to job creation in Newfoundland.
The benefits of any increased spending in the consumer-purchasing area are felt in Ontario and other areas where manufacturing industries are concentrated. This is, of course, concentrated in central Canada. That area of the country benefits from a policy such as the 3 per cent remission of sales tax, but not an area like Newfoundland, which does not have this type of industry.
The structure of the economy of Canada militates against Newfoundland ever improving its position in the Canadian federation. I quote from the report of the People's Commission on Unemployment in Newfoundland, released earlier this year, page 15:
Tariffs and import duties protect the market for Central Canadian industry, and government stimulants encourage consumption, but there is no such protection for producers or raw materials. If the Aluminum Company of Canada can get cheaper fluorspar in Mexico, the miners of St. Lawrence lose their jobs, but they and their families must still buy goods that are not produced in Newfoundland-
Transfer payments from Ottawa can be viewed as an indirect subsidy to Central Canadian industry: a subsidy which, while keeping Newfoundlanders alive, also serves to keep Newfoundland's economy underdeveloped.
The present structure tends to perpetuate the inequalities of income and opportunity that exist in this country with regard to an area like Newfoundland. Federal programs hailed by the minister as special considerations have been a dismal failure. The minister relied upon DREE as a program to help Newfoundland.
Let us look at DREE. When it was set up in 1969, its stated objective was to redistribute wealth from the have provinces to the have-not provinces on an enduring basis. What has been the result? Up until 1975, $185 million was spent to provide a total of about 3,400 jobs. The Economic Council of Canada in its 1977 report stated that in the period 1970-75 over 8,300 jobs were needed just to reduce unemployment in Newfoundland by one half of 1 per cent.
As for where the money was spent by DREE, I go back to the People's Commission report, page 70, and I quote:
Between 1969 and 1975 DREE spent more than 75 per cent of all its moneys in the province on what the Economic Council of Canada calls "non-rural infrastructure"-

November 13, 1978
Adjournment Debate
The commission finds nothing wrong with the construction of roads and the building of schools. But we must seriously raise the question as to whether DREE has, through its support of urban development, made our rural areas less competitive in terms of economic development and job creation.
DREE seems to have contributed to the non-viability of our rural areas without any redeeming contribution to our urban areas. In view of this type of situation, it is incumbent on the minister to give this House some concrete proposals as to what he is prepared to do in his forthcoming budget to realistically meet the pressing needs of the province of Newfoundland.
I call on the minister to bring in a new deal of a Marshall plan type of economic package that will radically change the position of Newfoundland within the Canadian economy so that real and lasting benefits might result.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT HAS SPECIAL ECONOMIC PROGRAM FOR NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to respond on behalf of my colleague the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) who has been unavoidably detained elsewhere this evening.
As the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Faour) indicated earlier, the Conference Board in Canada has forecast that real output in Newfoundland will decline by almost 2 per cent in 1978. However, it is important to note-as the Conference Board has done-that this contraction is in large part due to the protracted strike, which lasted from March to July, in Labrador's iron mines. Production has since resumed, and indeed the Conference Board forecasts a real growth of almost 4 per cent in 1979 which will more than recoup the losses of the previous two years. In spite of this decline in real output in 1978, the Conference Board also forecasts a growth of 2.9 per cent in employment in Newfoundland in 1978; but as in the case in the rest of the country,
the growth of the labour force is even greater and consequently the rate of unemployment has risen.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) indicated on October 30 when the hon. member first raised the question, the national and regional economic situations are taken into account when the budget is drafted. Moreover, as all hon. members know, the provisions of the budget are not discussed prior to the presentation of the budget, and hence they will have to wait until later this month for the budget.
I should, nevertheless, make note of a few points with regard to the request that some special economic program be set out for the province of Newfoundland. First, as I mentioned at the beginning in noting the Conference Board's forecast, this year's decline in real provincial output is in large part due to strike activity. This is now past and, more important, no structural change had occurred to bring this decline about; consequently, the need for special consideration does not arise because of this forecast decline.
Second, as the Minister of Finance stated on October 30, there already exist numerous provisions and measures which do provide help and incentives to those provinces such as Newfoundland which have higher than average unemployment rates and below-average per capita incomes.
Finally, I should remind the hon. member that the Economic Council of Canada has currently under way a major study of the Newfoundland economy; the government will wish to consider this study and its recommendations when it is completed, and subsequently take appropriate actions.
